chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Working Capital Really Is

lessons.title: Gross, Net and Operating Working Capital: Which Number Actually Matters

children.text: Ask three people in a company what the working capital is and you can get three different numbers, all of them correct. The chief financial officer quotes one, the bank's credit officer quotes another, and the equity analyst building a valuation model quotes a third. They are not disagreeing. They are answering different questions.
This lesson sorts out the three measures, shows what each one is good for, and then settles the question in the title: for running a business, one of them matters far more than the others.
Three Measures, One Balance Sheet

We will use the same company as the previous lesson, Sunrise Ceramics Ltd, so the lines are familiar: current assets of ₹122 crore, current liabilities of ₹101 crore, of which ₹42 crore is trade payables and ₹43 crore is bank borrowing.

body.title: Sunrise Ceramics: four ways to say working capital (₹ crore)

children.text: Look at the spread. The same company can be described as having ₹122 crore of working capital or ₹21 crore of it. Neither is wrong.
Gross working capital
counts everything in the operating block regardless of who funded it.
Net working capital
subtracts everything due within a year, including the bank's cash credit, which is why it collapses to ₹21 crore.

markDefs.definition: Total current assets, with no deduction for current liabilities. It measures how much sits in the operating block, not who funded it.
Current assets minus current liabilities. The headline measure of short-term financial cushion.

body.text: Whenever someone quotes a working capital figure, ask which measure it is before you react to it. A company that "cut working capital from ₹122 crore to ₹58 crore" may have changed nothing at all, and simply switched from the gross measure to the trade measure.

children.text: Why Operating Working Capital Is the One to Manage

Net working capital has a hole in it. It nets off cash and short-term borrowing, which are financing choices, not operating performance. Take a fresh ₹10 crore short-term loan and park it in the bank, and net working capital does not move at all: current assets and current liabilities both rise by ₹10 crore. Nothing about the business changed, yet the gross figure jumped.
Operating working capital

strips both out. It answers the only question a manager can act on: how many rupees does this business lock up in inventory, receivables, supplier credit and other operating items for every rupee of sales? For Sunrise Ceramics on FY2026 sales of ₹180 crore, that is ₹53.5 crore, or 29.7% of sales. The narrower trade measure of ₹58 crore works out to 32.2% of sales, which is about 118 days of sales stuck in the cycle.

markDefs.definition: Working capital from operations only, excluding cash and every form of borrowing. It measures how much the business itself locks up per rupee of sales.

stats.label: Trade working capital
stats.context: About 118 days of sales locked in inventory and receivables, net of supplier credit

stats.label: Net working capital
stats.context: Looks small only because the ₹43 crore of bank borrowing is netted off

body.text: Net working capital tells you how the operating block is funded today. Operating working capital tells you how big the block is. You can only manage the block.

body.title: Pick the right measure
body.question: You want to compare how efficiently two tile makers of different sizes run their operations. One is debt-free with a large cash pile, the other funds itself with a cash credit limit. Which measure should you compare?
options: Operating working capital as a percentage of sales
body.explanation: Operating working capital excludes cash and borrowing, so the two funding styles do not distort it, and expressing it as a percentage of sales removes the size difference. Rupee figures of any measure would mostly tell you which company is bigger.

body.title: Compute trade working capital
body.prompt: Deccan Polymers reports inventories of ₹26 crore, trade receivables of ₹34 crore, cash of ₹3 crore, other current assets of ₹5 crore, a cash credit balance of ₹22 crore, trade payables of ₹19 crore and other current liabilities of ₹9 crore. What is its trade working capital in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Trade working capital uses only the three core lines: ₹26 crore inventories plus ₹34 crore receivables minus ₹19 crore payables, which is ₹41 crore. For contrast, gross working capital is ₹68 crore and net working capital is only ₹18 crore, because the ₹22 crore cash credit is netted off.

children.text: Where Each Measure Actually Gets Used

columns.label: Bankers and credit teams
points: Start from the working capital gap: current assets minus current liabilities other than bank borrowing
For Sunrise Ceramics that gap is ₹64 crore
Traditional lending norms fund about 75% of it, here ₹48 crore, with the borrower bringing the rest as margin
The actual cash credit limit drawn is ₹35 crore, so there is headroom on this test

columns.label: Analysts and valuation teams
points: Use operating or trade working capital, never the net figure
What they care about is the change from year to year, not the level
An increase in operating working capital is a cash outflow in the cash flow statement
It reduces free cash flow rupee for rupee, which feeds straight into valuation

children.text: That second point is worth making concrete. Suppose Sunrise Ceramics grows next year and its operating working capital rises from ₹53.5 crore to ₹62 crore. The ₹8.5 crore increase is cash that left the business, and it appears as a negative movement in the operating section of the cash flow statement. It reduces
free cash flow
by exactly that amount, however good the profit line looks.

markDefs.definition: Cash left after a business funds its operations, its working capital and its capital expenditure. An increase in operating working capital reduces it rupee for rupee.

body.label: Working capital gap for a lender
body.context: Current assets of ₹122 crore minus non-bank current liabilities of ₹58.0 crore. Traditional norms fund about 75% of this gap, or ₹48 crore.

body.title: Why screener.in shows two very different numbers

children.text: On screener.in you will find both a cash conversion cycle and a working capital days figure in the Ratios section, and they often disagree sharply. For FY2026, Hindustan Unilever shows a cash conversion cycle of about -89 days against working capital days of about -23. Titan shows a cash conversion cycle of about 211 days against working capital days of about 28.

The reason is exactly what this lesson is about. The cash conversion cycle is built from the three trade lines alone: inventory, receivables and payables. Working capital days is built from the broader net working capital, which includes other current assets and other current liabilities such as customer advances, statutory dues and provisions. For a jeweller funding gold through customer advance schemes and gold metal loans, those other lines are huge, so the two measures tell different stories.
Neither figure is wrong. Use the cash conversion cycle to judge operating discipline in the trade lines, and the broader figure to judge the total funding need.

body.title: The improvement that was not one
body.scenario: A mid-sized pharma formulations company reports to its board that net working capital fell from ₹64 crore to ₹53 crore over the year, and calls it a major efficiency gain. Digging into the balance sheet, you find inventories rose from ₹52 crore to ₹58 crore, trade receivables rose from ₹71 crore to ₹79 crore, trade payables were flat at ₹44 crore, and the cash credit balance rose from ₹28 crore to ₹53 crore.
body.prompt: Did operations actually improve? Work out what really happened and what you would tell the board.
body.modelAnswer:
Operations got worse, not better. Trade working capital rose from ₹52 crore plus ₹71 crore minus ₹44 crore, which is ₹79 crore, to ₹58 crore plus ₹79 crore minus ₹44 crore, which is ₹93 crore. That is ₹14 crore more cash locked in inventory and receivables.

Net working capital fell by ₹11 crore only because the company borrowed ₹25 crore more on its cash credit limit, and that borrowing is a current liability that gets netted off. The business did not release cash. It financed a bigger operating block with more short-term debt.

What to tell the board: report trade or operating working capital alongside the net figure, and track it as a percentage of sales. Then ask the two real questions, which are why inventory grew faster than sales and why receivables did the same. Ask also how much headroom is left on the cash credit limit, because that is now the only thing holding the cycle up.

body.title: Name the measure
body.textWithBlank: The measure that excludes cash and all short-term borrowing, so that it reflects only what operations lock up, is called ___ working capital.
body.explanation: Operating working capital removes both cash and borrowings, which are financing choices, leaving only the inventory, receivables, payables and other operating lines that managers can actually act on.

children.text: Fix the Vocabulary

body.title: The four measures, side by side

cards.definition: Total current assets, with nothing deducted. Shows the size of the operating block but not who funds it.
Current assets minus current liabilities. The headline cushion figure, distorted by cash and short-term debt.
Inventories plus trade receivables minus trade payables. The three core operating lines only.
All non-cash current assets minus all non-debt current liabilities. What operations lock up per rupee of sales.
Current assets minus current liabilities other than bank borrowing. The lender's starting point for sizing a limit.
The year-on-year movement in operating working capital. An increase is a cash outflow and reduces free cash flow.

body.label: Compare the measures on a real company
body.description: Open the Ratios section and read the cash conversion cycle and working capital days rows side by side, then check the balance sheet above them. The gap between the two rows is the gap between the trade measure and the net measure.

points: Gross working capital is total current assets, net working capital deducts all current liabilities, and operating working capital deducts only the non-financing ones.
Net working capital is distorted by cash and short-term borrowing, so it is a poor measure of operating performance.
Operating and trade working capital are the measures a manager can act on, and both are best read as a percentage of sales.
Lenders work from the working capital gap, which excludes bank borrowing from current liabilities, and traditionally fund about 75% of it.
Analysts care about the change in operating working capital, because an increase is a direct cash outflow that reduces free cash flow.
Always ask which measure a working capital number refers to before comparing it with anything else.
